author: dzekojohn4
body:
## Labels / Complexity
`bug` · `events` · `validation` · `High Complexity`

## Problem

The event tooling generates *two* overlapping artifacts that are not kept in agreement:

- `scripts/events/generate-registry.mjs` produces `schemas/events/registry.json` (`OUT_REGISTRY` at `scripts/events/generate-registry.mjs:7`) plus `docs/EVENTS.md`.
- `scripts/events/generate-schemas.mjs` produces `schemas/events/event-schema-registry.json` plus one `schemas/events/*_event.schema.json` per event.

The twist is that the validator validates the first registry, which the repository does **not** track:

```text
$ git ls-files schemas/events/ | grep registry
schemas/events/event-schema-registry.json
```

Only `event-schema-registry.json` is tracked; `schemas/events/registry.json` is generated but never committed. Meanwhile `scripts/events/validate.mjs` does:

```js
const registry = await loadJson("schemas/events/registry.json");
```

Consequences:

- **CI validates a phantom artifact.** The gate described by `validate.mjs` checks `registry.json`, which exists only transiently on a machine that just ran the generator; on a fresh checkout it is absent and the validate step cannot run as intended.
- **Two registries drift silently.** `registry.json` (assessed by the validator) and `event-schema-registry.json` (the tracked, reviewed artifact) are produced by two separate generators with different logic, so a change to a contract's events can update one and not the other, and nothing fails.
- **The M1 extractor cannot trust a single source of truth.** The trace schema and the extractor must validate against one registry; today which one is authoritative is ambiguous and the tracked one has no validation gate.

## Root cause

```js
// scripts/events/validate.mjs — validates a generated, untracked file
const registry = await loadJson("schemas/events/registry.json");
```

```js
// scripts/events/generate-registry.mjs:7
const OUT_REGISTRY = path.join(REPO_ROOT, "schemas", "events", "registry.json");
// but generate-schemas.mjs writes event-schema-registry.json instead
```

Two generators, two filenames, one validation path pointing at the untracked one.

## Why this is architecturally hard

1. **The naive fix (commit `registry.json`) papers over the fork.** Both files would still be generated by separate scripts that can disagree; committing one makes the drift a lint failure rather than removing the second generator. The real question is which artifact is canonical for the M1 extractor and why there are two.
2. **The generators scan source differently.** `generate-registry.mjs` and `generate-schemas.mjs` each implement their own Rust-source scan (topic parsing, payload-width inference). Reconciling them is a correctness change to how events are derived from `contracts/**`, not a file-copy fix. `scripts/check_events.sh` (the `pub fn` audit) is a third, independent scan of the same source that must end up consistent.
3. **The schema files are hand-maintained on top of generated ones.** `schemas/events/*_event.schema.json` (e.g. `record_created_event.schema.json`) sit beside generated code and are not obviously regenerated in lockstep, so trace records validated against them can disagree with the registry enum of topics.
4. **The M1 trace schema must hook into one authoritative source.** A trace-extraction validation gate needs a single registry to test against; until the sources converge, new trace schemas will inherit the ambiguity.

## Proposed design

- Designate one generator and one committed artifact as canonical (recommend the tracked `event-schema-registry.json` plus `docs/EVENTS.md`), and have `validate.mjs` regenerate-and-diff against the canonical file instead of reading an untracked path.
- Make the schema generation and the registry generation share a single source-scan, so a topic in one is a topic in the other with no hand reconciliation.
- Add a CI workflow (there is no `.github/workflows` currently) that runs the canonical validate step on pull requests.

## Acceptance criteria

### Canonical source

- [ ] One committed JSON artifact is the single authoritative event registry, and `docs/EVENTS.md` is regenerated from it via a single generator.
- [ ] `scripts/events/validate.mjs` validates the canonical, tracked artifact (regenerate-and-diff) and fails cleanly if it is stale, rather than reading a transient untracked file.

### Convergence

- [ ] A change to an emitted event topic in any `contracts/*/src/*.rs` updates exactly one scan and the regenerated registry + schema set stay identical to each other with no manual edits.

### Tests / CI

- [ ] `npm run events:validate` and `npm run events:generate` pass on a fresh checkout with no pre-existing generated files.
- [ ] A CI workflow runs the validation gate and fails on drift.

## Out of scope

Authoring the new `ContractTrace` JSON schema and its validation gate (separate M1 feature). This issue converges the *existing* registry/schema sources so the new schema has a single thing to attach to.

## Getting started

- `scripts/events/generate-registry.mjs`
- `scripts/events/generate-schemas.mjs`
- `scripts/events/validate.mjs`
- `schemas/events/` (tracked: `event-schema-registry.json`, per-event schemas; untracked: `registry.json`)
- `package.json` (`events:generate`, `events:validate`)

Run and verify: `npm run events:generate`, `npm run events:validate`.

Good first files to read:
- `scripts/events/generate-registry.mjs`
- `scripts/events/generate-schemas.mjs`
- `scripts/events/validate.mjs`
title: schemas/events registry has two divergent generated sources, and validate.mjs checks a file the repo does not track

author: dzekojohn4
body:
## Labels / Complexity
`enhancement` · `api-design` · `validation` · `specifications` · `High Complexity`

## Context

Every artifact an off-chain system builds on top of contract execution — dashboards, replay, audit, fuzzing — depends on a stable description of what a trace looks like. No such description exists. The repo has a rich event vocabulary (`docs/EVENTS.md`, auto-generated; `schemas/events/*_event.schema.json`; `schemas/events/event_envelope.schema.json`) and a serialization standard (`docs/SERIALIZATION_STANDARDS.md`), but nothing defines the shape of a *trace*: the ordered, correlated record of one Soroban invocation that binds its function, arguments, return value, and emitted events together. The telemetry correlation mechanism in `docs/TELEMETRY_SCHEMA.md` implies such a record but the schema is undefined.

Because the trace shape is undefined, every consumer names its fields differently. The M1 extractor, the fuzz recorder, and the CLI cannot share output, and no gate can catch a consumer whose decoder drops a field. A hardcoded per-tool trace shape is the maintenance trap: it fossilizes one implementation's assumptions and disconnects from the auto-generated `docs/EVENTS.md` registry the moment a contract emits a new topic.

## Goal

Define the canonical JSON schema for a `ContractTrace` (one per invocation) in `schemas/`, validate the M1 extractor's NDJSON output against it in CI, and keep it linked to the authoritative event registry so a new emitted topic is either added to the schema or fails validation.

## Scope

### 1. Trace schema
Author a JSON Schema document describing one `ContractTrace`: `trace_id` (the cross-contract linking key), contract id, function symbol, typed arguments and return value, the ordered list of events (each conforming to the existing `event_envelope.schema.json`), and the raw result XDR (optional) for auditability. Version it so a breaking field change is explicit.

### 2. Registry linkage
Define a per-event "trace contract" (which event may appear under which function, and its topic) derived from the authoritative registry from the M1 registry-convergence issue, so the schema cannot silently accept topics the registry does not contain.

### 3. NDJSON validation harness
Add a validator (Node, consistent with `scripts/events/validate.mjs`) that reads the M1 CLI extractor's NDJSON/JSONL output line-by-line and validates each record against the schema and the registry, exiting non-zero on the first violation.

### 4. CI gate
Wire the validator into a workflow so the extractor output can never drift from the schema; since no `.github/workflows` exists today, this establishes the pattern.

## Acceptance criteria

### Schema

- [ ] `schemas/trace/contract_trace.schema.json` (or an equivalent documented path) describes a single `ContractTrace` with `trace_id`, function, ordered events, and typed argument/return fields, and is versioned.
- [ ] Every event object inside a `ContractTrace` validates against the existing `schemas/events/event_envelope.schema.json`.

### Validity / linkage

- [ ] A sample extractor NDJSON record for a known contract validates with zero manual edits.
- [ ] A record whose `trace_id` is not a 32-byte hex identifier, or whose event topics are absent from the authoritative registry, fails validation.

### CI / tests

- [ ] The NDJSON validator is runnable and wired into a workflow; a deliberately malformed record causes a non-zero exit.
- [ ] `npm run` validation targets pass and the validator is lintable via `make shellcheck` if it touches shell.

## Out of scope

The trace decoder library, the CLI extractor, and the event-registry convergence are separate M1 issues. This issue only defines the schema and the gate that keeps extractor output conformant.

## Getting started

- `schemas/events/event_envelope.schema.json` and the per-event `*_event.schema.json` to reuse as `$ref` targets.
- `scripts/events/validate.mjs` — the AJV-based validation pattern to mirror.
- `schemas/events/event-schema-registry.json` — the authoritative registry to reference for topics.
- `package.json` — where an `npm run` target for the new validator would be added.

Run and verify: `npm run events:validate`, then run the new validator over sample NDJSON.

Good first files to read:
- `schemas/events/event_envelope.schema.json`
- `scripts/events/validate.mjs`
- `docs/TELEMETRY_SCHEMA.md` (the trace/correlation vocabulary the schema formalizes)
title: Feature: ContractTrace JSON Schema And Validation Gate

author: dzekojohn4
body:
## Labels / Complexity
`bug` · `serialization` · `standardization` · `High Complexity`

## Problem

`docs/SERIALIZATION_STANDARDS.md` declares the canonical encoding rules every contract must follow, but nothing in the repository checks conformance. The document codifies rules such as:

```markdown
### 2. `Map` ordering
`soroban_sdk::Map` preserves insertion order in XDR. When comparing maps across
versions, always compare keys explicitly rather than byte-level equality.

### 1. `Option<T>` encoding
`Option<T>` serialises as `SCVal::Void` for `None` and `SCVal::T` for `Some(T)`.
Do **not** use sentinel values (e.g. `u64::MAX` for "no value") — use `Option`.
```

Yet a console-greppable search finds no test, script, or lint in the repo that asserts any contract conforms. The only XDR operations are the encode-side uses of `ToXdr` in `contracts/meta_tx_forwarder/src/lib.rs:29` and the audit hash builders (`contracts/audit/src/lib.rs:507`, `:778`). There is no ABI/round-trip conformance suite tied to these rules.

For the M1 trace-extraction milestone this is a machine-failure latent defect. The off-chain decoder must translate `SCVal` encoded by each contract into typed Rust/JSON values. The decoder's correctness depends on contracts honoring the standard:

- **Sentinel-vs-`Option` ambiguity.** A contract that encodes "no value" as `u64::MAX` (the rule explicitly forbids) produces a decoded *sentinel number* indistinguishable from a real value, so an extracted trace asserts the wrong state.
- **`Map` ordering drift.** A trace that compares two versions of a record byte-for-byte (as the rule forbids) misreads reordered keys as a content change, corrupting trace diffs and round-trip fidelity checks in the fuzz harness.
- **`Symbol`-as-`u32` fragmentation.** `docs/SERIALIZATION_STANDARDS.md` canonical mapping says enumerated state must be `#[contracttype] enum`, never raw `u32` in the ABI (per the rule "Enumerated state | `#[contracttype] enum` | Never raw u32 in ABI"). Any contract passing a bare `u32` creates a topic/payload the extractor cannot interpret without per-contract knowledge.

Today a contract that deviates merely produces a trace that is *wrong*, not a build that fails — silent incorrectness at the boundary the M1 milestone depends on.

## Root cause

```markdown
# docs/SERIALIZATION_STANDARDS.md
The document is normative text with no executable counterpart; no gate runs
against contract ABIs, so an `Option`/`Map`/`enum` deviation compiles, deploys,
and only surfaces as wrong decoded values in the extractor.
```

A standard with no conformance check is a comment, not a constraint.

## Why this is architecturally hard

1. **The naive shortcut (spot-check `events()` payloads) is not general.** Conformance must be checkable across 100+ contracts (`contracts/` holds over a hundred crates) and across their cross-contract ABI boundaries, not just in a handful of tests. A targeted audit passes while the general boundary stays unverified.
2. **The rule set is heterogeneous and partly non-computable.** `Map`-ordering ("compare keys explicitly") is a *consumer* discipline, not something a scanner can prove about arbitrary code. Distinguishing "forbidden sentinel" from "legitimate use" requires semantic knowledge. The conformance layer must separate mechanically-checkable rules (raw `u32` in ABI, missing `#[contracttype]`) from testable behavioral rules (round-trip stability).
3. **It must integrate with the M1 decoder contract.** The conformance suite's round-trip baseline is exactly what the `libs` decoder asserts on golden XDR. These two features must share fixtures, or the decoder can claim success against non-conforming output that real contracts would never produce.
4. **Introducing a gate that fails on existing contracts is a migration.** Enforcing the rules unconditionally will surface pre-existing deviations across the workspace (many contracts sit excluded from the workspace build per the `exclude` list in `Cargo.toml`). The PR must scope the gate (new/changed ABIs first) rather than attempt a whole-repo sweep.

## Proposed design

- Add a conformance harness (Rust integration tests under `tests/`, following the existing `tests/event_validation.rs` / `tests/event_system_test.rs` pattern) with two tiers: (a) mechanical ABI checks (no raw `u32` enumerated ABI where `#[contracttype] enum` is required; `Option` types not shadowed by sentinel constants) and (b) a round-trip suite asserting that serializing and deserializing representative `SCVal`s is byte-stable across the canonical types in the standard.
- Share the XDR fixtures and `SCVal` → typed mapping with the `libs` trace decoder so both verify the same encoding contract.
- Scope enforcement to workspace-member contracts first; excluded contracts (per `Cargo.toml` `exclude`) are tracked as follow-up, not forced in this PR.

## Acceptance criteria

### Conformance harness

- [ ] A `tests/` integration suite checks the canonical rules from `docs/SERIALIZATION_STANDARDS.md` (Option/Void vs sentinel, Map key ordering, enum-over-u32, bounded strings) for the workspace-member contracts and fails on a represented sample violation.
- [ ] `Option::None`/`Some` round-trips through XDR without sentinel ambiguity, and a fixture proving this is committed.

### Decoder alignment

- [ ] The conformance suite and the `libs` trace decoder share the same golden XDR fixtures, and the decoder's `SCVal` mapping covers every canonical type named in the standard.

### Scoping / CI

- [ ] The gate runs on changed contracts only (new/changed ABI), so it does not block on pre-existing workspace-excluded deviations, and it is wired into CI.
- [ ] `cargo test --workspace` and `make lint` pass with the suite in place.

## Out of scope

Conformance enforcement across the ~dozens of workspace-`exclude`d contracts in `Cargo.toml`, and any rewrite of running contracts to satisfy rules they currently violate; those are tracked separately.

## Getting started

- `docs/SERIALIZATION_STANDARDS.md` — the normative rule set to encode as checks.
- `tests/event_validation.rs` and `tests/event_system_test.rs` — the existing integration-test pattern to mirror (same directory, same `cargo test --test` wiring).
- `Cargo.toml` — the workspace `members`/`exclude` split that defines the initial gate scope.

Run and verify: `make test-integration`, `cargo test --workspace`, `make lint`.

Good first files to read:
- `docs/SERIALIZATION_STANDARDS.md`
- `tests/event_validation.rs`
- `Cargo.toml` (members / exclude)
title: XDR serialization conformance is documented but unenforced, so cross-contract trace decoding can fail silently

# Compression-Oracle Side-Channel Mitigation for At-Rest Envelope Compression

**Labels:** `extremely-hard` `hard` `security` `cryptography` `Official Campaign` `Maybe Rewarded`
**Component:** `src/storage/db.rs`, builds on `#056` (envelope compression at rest), `#051` (constant-time signing/lookups), `#012` (encryption at rest)

---

## Problem

Issue `#056` compresses envelopes before `#012` encrypts them at rest, which is the standard "compress-then-encrypt" pipeline shape — and it's also the exact shape behind the CRIME and BREACH attacks against TLS. Any time a compression stream mixes attacker-influenceable plaintext (e.g. a `memo` field a co-located malicious app can indirectly cause this device to write, by initiating payments to it that this device then queues) with secret plaintext in the same compression context (destination account, amount, or other fields whose value an attacker wants to learn), the *compressed size* becomes a side channel: an attacker who can trigger many envelope writes with chosen memo content and observe resulting ciphertext lengths (via file sizes, backup sizes, or timing of writes) can perform a byte-at-a-time oracle attack to recover the secret field, because a guessed byte that matches the secret compresses better and produces a shorter output. This is a real, well-documented vulnerability class, not a theoretical one, and `#056` as scoped doesn't address it.

## Requirements

- Analyze `#056`'s actual compression scheme (dictionary usage, stream boundaries, which fields are compressed together) for compression-oracle exposure: identify every case where attacker-influenceable content and secret content share a compression context.
- Implement a mitigation appropriate to the finding — options include separating attacker-influenceable fields into their own compression context from secret fields, disabling compression selectively for fields where the length side channel matters most, padding compressed output to fixed-size buckets to reduce (not necessarily eliminate — be honest about residual leakage) the signal, or using a fixed, non-adaptive compression dictionary that doesn't respond to attacker-chosen content. Justify the choice against the actual attacker model for this crate (a co-located malicious app or a party who can observe backup file sizes, not a network attacker).
- Quantify residual leakage after mitigation: implement a measurement harness that attempts the byte-at-a-time oracle attack against the mitigated implementation and reports how many bits of a secret field it can recover, if any, over a defined number of chosen-plaintext attempts.
- Document the threat model and residual risk plainly — overclaiming "fixed" when the real result is "leakage reduced from N bits to M bits" is worse than an honest partial result.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Every point where attacker-influenceable and secret plaintext share a compression context is identified and documented.
- [ ] A mitigation is implemented and its rationale documented against this crate's actual attacker model.
- [ ] A measurement harness attempts the oracle attack against both the unmitigated and mitigated implementations and reports quantified results for both.
- [ ] `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy -D warnings`, and `cargo test` all pass.

### Required Tests

- [ ] **`test_unmitigated_baseline_leaks_secret_byte_via_compressed_length`** (demonstrates the vulnerability exists before your fix, for regression tracking)
- [ ] **`test_mitigated_implementation_reduces_oracle_signal`**
- [ ] **`test_attacker_influenceable_and_secret_fields_use_separate_compression_contexts`**
- [ ] **`test_compression_still_provides_meaningful_size_reduction_after_mitigation`** (guards against a mitigation so aggressive it defeats `#056`'s original purpose)

## Notes

- Depends on `#056`'s compression scheme and `#012`'s encryption pipeline both being stable to analyze against. Please open a design discussion first with your context-separation analysis before implementing the fix.
- Estimated effort: **extreme**.
title: Compression-Oracle Side-Channel Mitigation for At-Rest Envelope Compression

> **Join the Telegram group (mandatory):** https://t.me/+j7ZXXQq8lpM2ZmQ0 — fastest way to reach the maintainer, ask questions, and stay in sync with the community.

> **Quality bar — this is a code contribution.** Build and test locally before you open a PR. Frontend: `npm install --legacy-peer-deps && npm run build`. Everything is manually reviewed — copy-paste, untested, or AI-generated filler gets closed, and farming = banned from the group + never assigned again (and can be flagged on GrantFox).

### 📝 Description

Four bugs found on the **Analytics page** during GrantFox Third Campaign QA (PR #14 ). FlowSummary renders a bare comma when assets is undefined, fetchXlmPrice is duplicated 3-4 times per page load, and chart panels have gaps/ambiguous labels.

**Cross-reference:** Original QA report in [PR #14](https://github.com/StellarVhibes/FluxID/pull/14) — Issue #7.

---

### Bug 1 — FlowSummary Assets stat renders bare comma (HIGH)

**Severity:** HIGH
**File:** `frontend/app/components/FlowSummary.tsx:143`

**Description:** When the `assets` prop is undefined, the Assets stat card renders a bare `,` — a copy-paste artifact. This is the first thing users see on the analytics overview.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] Assets stat card renders "0" or "—" when assets is undefined/null
- [ ] No bare punctuation rendered in any stat card
- [ ] Stat cards handle all edge cases: undefined, null, 0, empty array

---

### Bug 2 — fetchXlmPrice duplicated 3-4 times per page load (MEDIUM)

**Severity:** MEDIUM
**Files:** `FlowSummary.tsx`, `AssetBreakdown.tsx`, `FlowChart.tsx`, `analytics/page.tsx`

**Description:** `fetchXlmPrice()` is copy-pasted into 4 separate components. Each fires its own CoinGecko request on page load — 3-4 concurrent identical API calls. This wastes quota and risks rate-limiting.

**Acceptance Criteria:**

**File:** `frontend/app/components/FlowChart.tsx`

### Bug 4 — Week labels ambiguous across year boundary (LOW)

Everything is manually reviewed — copy-paste, untested, or AI-generated filler gets closed, and farming = banned from the group + never assigned again (and can be flagged on GrantFox).

### 📝 Description

Six bugs found on the **Dashboard score and on-chain save** during GrantFox Third Campaign QA (PR #16 ). The score orb animation is broken, save on-chain has a DNS failure (CRITICAL), Recent Flow shows only ~30 transactions, and several minor issues with assets and feedback.

**Cross-reference:** Original QA report in [PR #16](https://github.com/StellarVhibes/FluxID/pull/16) — Issue #6.

---

### Bug 1 — Score orb center number stuck at 0 (HIGH)

**Severity:** HIGH
**File:** `AnimatedScore` component

**Description:** After re-analysis, the score orb center number stays at `0` while the SVG ring reflects the real score. This is intermittent — sometimes the number updates, sometimes it doesn't.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] Center number always matches the SVG ring score
- [ ] After re-analysis, the number updates (no stale 0)
- [ ] Animation completes smoothly without visual glitches

---

### Bug 2 — Save on-chain DNS failure (CRITICAL)

**Severity:** CRITICAL
**File:** `backend/src/config/stellar.config.ts`

**Description:** Save on-chain completely fails. The backend uses `rpc.testnet.stellar.org` which does not resolve DNS. The correct public Soroban RPC is `soroban-testnet.stellar.org`. Same issue exists for mainnet (`rpc.mainnet.stellar.org` should be `soroban-mainnet.stellar.org`).

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] Testnet RPC endpoint changed to `soroban-testnet.stellar.org`
- [ ] Mainnet RPC endpoint changed to `soroban-mainnet.stellar.org`
- [ ] Save on-chain completes successfully on testnet
- [ ] Transaction hash is captured and returned to frontend
- [ ] Error handling for RPC failures (timeout, rate limit, etc.)

---

### Bug 3 — Recent Flow shows only ~30 transactions (MEDIUM)

**Severity:** MEDIUM
**File:** Recent Flow component

**Description:** The Recent Flow section shows only the newest ~30 transactions from Horizon, while the overall insight sees all transactions. This creates a misleading picture.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] Recent Flow shows the most recent transactions (up to a reasonable limit, e.g., 50-100)
- [ ] Or: show "Showing 30 of 500 transactions" with pagination/see more
- [ ] No contradiction between Recent Flow count and overall stats

---

### Bug 4 — Decorative orb PNG has hardcoded "82" (LOW)

**Severity:** LOW
**File:** `docs/` (assets)

**Description:** The decorative orb PNG `fluxid_trust_score_orb.png` has a faint hardcoded "82" that reads as a second score alongside the real score.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] Remove the "82" from the orb asset, or use a blank orb
- [ ] Orb is purely decorative and does not display any numbers

---

### Bug 5 — Network toggle keeps stale analysis visible (LOW)

**Severity:** LOW
**File:** Network toggle logic

**Description:** Switching between mainnet/testnet keeps the previous analysis visible until Analyze is clicked again. Additionally, Save on-chain enables from the toggle alone, allowing stale data to be saved to the wrong network.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] Switching network clears the previous analysis
- [ ] Save on-chain is disabled until a new analysis is completed on the selected network
- [ ] Clear visual indicator when analysis is stale (wrong network)

---

### Bug 6 — Feedback submit hangs (LOW)

**Severity:** LOW
**File:** Feedback submit handler

**Description:** The in-app feedback button stays on "Sending…" for a long time. Direct POST to the endpoint succeeds instantly. Possible hung client promise or missing timeout.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] Feedback submit has a reasonable timeout (e.g., 10s)
- [ ] On timeout, show "Failed to send — try again" with retry option
- [ ] Success state is shown immediately after POST completes

---

  - Backend: `cd backend && npm run build`

author: karagozemin
body:
## Problem

The web hex decoder treats an empty string or bare prefix as a valid empty byte array. In the auditor flow those values represent missing key or blob input and only fail later with a less useful cryptography error.

## Task

Reject empty hex payloads with the existing invalid-hex error and add focused helper tests.

## Acceptance criteria

- Empty, whitespace-only, and prefix-only inputs are rejected.
- Valid prefixed and unprefixed hex still decode correctly.
- The helper tests are included in the normal web test command.
- Web tests and typecheck pass.

## Suggested implementation prompt

> Add focused tests for the web hex helper, reject empty decoded payloads while preserving valid hex behavior, include the test in the web test command, and keep the change limited to this helper contract.
title: fix(web): reject empty hex input in the auditor decoder

author: karagozemin
body:
## Problem

Existing GitHub Actions jobs have no `timeout-minutes` limit. A hung dependency install, contract build, or test can consume runner time indefinitely.

## Task

Add a reasonable explicit timeout to every existing workflow job without changing steps or triggers.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every workflow job has a finite timeout.
- Contract and binding jobs retain enough time for a cold Rust build.
- Steps, triggers, permissions, and action versions are unchanged.
- Workflow YAML remains valid.

## Suggested implementation prompt

> Add conservative explicit job timeouts to every existing workflow, allowing extra room for cold Rust builds, validate the YAML, and change nothing else.
title: ci: add explicit timeouts to workflow jobs

## Problem

Local Node coverage runs can leave standard coverage directories and LCOV files untracked because the repository ignore rules do not cover them.

## Task

Ignore local coverage output while keeping committed fixtures and configuration visible.

## Acceptance criteria

- Standard coverage directories and LCOV report files are ignored.
- No existing tracked file becomes unintentionally hidden.
- Only ignore rules change.

## Problem

The repository enforces LF endings for several source formats but omits shell scripts, workflow YAML, CSS, and HTML. Those files can acquire CRLF endings and break shell execution or create noisy diffs.

## Task

Extend the existing attributes rules to cover the omitted first-party text formats.

## Acceptance criteria

- Shell, YAML, CSS, and HTML files are explicitly normalized to LF.
- Existing attribute rules remain unchanged.
- No source file is reformatted in this PR.

## Suggested implementation prompt

> Add LF text rules for the omitted script, workflow, and web text formats to the attributes file, verify the rules with Git, and do not renormalize unrelated files.
title: chore(gitattributes): enforce LF endings for scripts and web assets

author: karagozemin
body:
## Problem

`validateEncryptedBlob` documents an explicit `hex` or `base64` encoding option but always auto-detects input. A value valid in the other encoding can therefore be accepted despite the caller requirement.

## Task

Respect the explicit encoding option and use auto-detection only when no encoding is supplied.

## Acceptance criteria

- Forced hex accepts only valid hex.
- Forced base64 accepts only valid base64.
- Omitted encoding retains auto-detection.
- Existing encrypted-blob tests, SDK tests, and typecheck pass.

## Suggested implementation prompt

> Fix encrypted-blob validation so the explicit encoding option selects exactly one decoder, add or adjust focused tests, run SDK validation, and keep the change scoped.
title: fix(sdk): honor the requested encrypted-blob encoding

author: karagozemin
body:
## Problem

`normalizeRoundId` validates decimal strings as positive, but returns bigint values without validation and accepts zero, negative, or unsafe numeric values through other branches.

## Task

Apply the same positive-integer contract to string, number, and bigint inputs. Reject unsafe JavaScript integers before conversion and add focused tests.

## Acceptance criteria

- Zero and negative number or bigint inputs are rejected.
- Unsafe, fractional, and non-finite numbers are rejected.
- Existing valid inputs remain unchanged.
- SDK tests and typecheck pass.

## Suggested implementation prompt

> Make SDK round ID normalization enforce one positive safe-integer contract across string, number, and bigint inputs, add boundary tests, and keep the diff limited to the helper and tests.
title: fix(sdk): validate numeric and bigint round IDs consistently

author: karagozemin
body:
## Problem

Appraisal API configuration accepts RPC URLs containing a username or password. Embedded credentials can leak through diagnostics, process inspection, or copied configuration.

## Task

Reject HTTP or HTTPS RPC URLs whose parsed URL contains credentials. Preserve all existing URL and network behavior.

## Acceptance criteria

- URLs with a username, password, or both are rejected with an `AppraisalConfigError`.
- Normal HTTP and HTTPS RPC URLs remain valid.
- The error does not echo credential contents.
- Appraisal configuration tests and typecheck pass.

## Suggested implementation prompt

> Add credential checks to appraisal RPC URL parsing, write focused tests for username and password URLs plus a valid control case, ensure errors do not reveal credentials, and keep the diff scoped.
title: fix(appraisal): reject credentials embedded in RPC URLs

The asset validator defines a seven-decimal stroop limit but applies the generic token limit to native assets, so invalid native configurations with more than seven decimals are accepted.

## Task

- SAC assets retain their current supported range.
- Existing valid fixtures still pass.
- SDK tests and typecheck pass.

## Suggested implementation prompt

> Apply the existing native stroop decimal constant when validating native assets, preserve the SAC limit, add boundary tests for both asset types, and make no unrelated changes.
title: fix(sdk): enforce the native asset decimal limit

author: oche2920
body:
## Summary
The coordinator reconciliation flow is implemented in `coordinator/src/reconciliation/reconciler.ts`, with cursor and lookback logic in `coordinator/src/reconciliation/ledger-cursor.ts`. The repo already has a replay model and metrics, but the current system still relies on best-effort windowing and partial recovery heuristics rather than an explicit, provable re-sync contract.

This is a high-risk reliability bug surface for a cross-chain bridge: when a chain falls behind, a restart occurs, or RPC responses are stale or partial, the reconciliation layer can silently lose or re-interpret events while active orders are still live. That creates real correctness risk for order settlement, secret reveal routing, and recovery behavior.

## Scope
- Rebuild the reconciliation pipeline as a formal replay/recovery policy across Ethereum, Soroban, and Solana.
- Add a deterministic event identity model to suppress duplicates without losing real updates.
- Define explicit gap-handling semantics when the cursor exceeds the lookback window or active orders are ahead of the known cursor.
- Implement resumable recovery on startup and after transient RPC failures without silent event loss.
- Add operator-grade reporting for replay window sizes, cursor lag, gap exceedance, conflict classification, and forced historical re-sync decisions.
- Validate the full path against the coordinator’s order lifecycle and event processors.

## Acceptance criteria
- The system recovers cleanly after a restart without silent event loss.
- Large gaps beyond the configured lookback window yield explicit warnings and deterministic recovery behavior.
- Duplicate or re-ordered events do not mutate order state incorrectly.
- Recovery is idempotent and safe under partial RPC outage or stale cursor state.
- Operators can inspect gap, replay, and conflict metrics without reconstructing event streams manually.
- The project includes regression tests for restart, gap, replay, and conflict scenarios.

## Testing requirements
- Unit tests for cursor fallback and gap calculations.
- Integration tests simulating missing event windows and delayed chain tip movement.
- Restart tests for stale or partial cursor state.
- Coverage target: at least 90% of reconciliation logic and 85% of branch paths exercised.
- Include failure scenarios for RPC reset/retry, chain gap larger than lookback, duplicate event delivery, and active orders with stale cursor values.

## Out of scope
- The public order API itself.
- Non-reconciliation operational tooling unrelated to replay correctness.

## Estimated effort
14 days

## Reward
rewarded

This is a full backend reliability project spanning cross-chain event replay, cursor correctness, and outage recovery. In a bridge system, missing or misordered events are a correctness bug with direct operational and financial impact, so the engineering and validation burden is substantial.
title: Rebuild the coordinator reconciliation engine into a formally provable event replay and gap-recovery system

author: oche2920
body:
## Summary
The HTLC contract in `soroban/contracts/htlc/src/lib.rs` already includes a `version` field on `Order`, TTL management, governance, and operational mode checks. The contract also has test coverage in `soroban/contracts/htlc/src/test.rs`, `soroban/contracts/htlc/src/harness.rs`, and `soroban/contracts/htlc/src/prop_tests.rs`.

However, there is no formal migration framework, upgrade-safe data transform path, or compatibility matrix for persisted order layouts and config keys. This makes future contract upgrades a high-risk operation that can silently break state interpretation or lock users out of claim/refund windows.

## Scope
- Design and implement a formal migration strategy for persisted HTLC order state and config keys.
- Add explicit schema-version gates for old and new ledger layouts, including incompatible upgrade detection.
- Implement safe migration/upgrade code paths for `Order` layout changes, config key changes, admin and pending-admin state transitions, and TTL-related archival assumptions.
- Guard future version changes so they cannot silently deserialize mixed-version state into invalid logic.
- Add migration-aware event emissions so indexers can detect schema changes and handle them correctly.
- Build a migration test harness covering legacy storage reads, mixed-version state handling, partial migration recovery, and post-upgrade invariant checks.

## Acceptance criteria
- Legacy orders created under the current layout remain readable and settle correctly after the migration logic runs.
- No contract call silently deserializes a mixed-version state into invalid order semantics.
- Migration failures leave the contract in a recoverable state and emit auditable event/log data.
- Successive upgrades are version-gated and cannot bypass required compatibility checks.
- The contract test suite includes a migration regression framework for old-state reads, in-place upgrades, and backwards compatibility.

## Testing requirements
- Unit tests for schema version checks and compatibility transitions.
- Property/fuzz tests for old/new layout coexistence and impossible state regressions.
- Integration tests simulating ledger state upgrades and order settlement before/after migration.
- Coverage target: 90% line coverage for migration logic, 85% branch coverage for upgrade paths.
- Include edge cases for partially migrated state, admin role change during migration, expired orders under legacy layouts, and mismatched config keys.

## Out of scope
- Rewriting HTLC business logic or changing timelock semantics.
- Multi-contract migration work outside the Soroban HTLC itself.

## Estimated effort
12 days

## Reward
rewarded

This is a high-risk contract-hardening issue because persisted-state compatibility is one of the most expensive failure modes in on-chain systems: a bad upgrade can strand funds, break settlement windows, or create silent logic drift. It requires deep Soroban storage reasoning and a broad migration regression suite, which is exactly the kind of principal-level work that warrants a funded contribution.
title: Harden Soroban HTLC storage and migration safety for future contract upgrades

author: misrasamuelisiguzor-oss
body:
## Description
Every Stellar Wave issue in this repo (247 of the last 249) follows the same Description / Requirements and context / Suggested execution / Example commit message / Guidelines structure, but `.github/` has no `ISSUE_TEMPLATE` directory, meaning the format is maintained purely by convention/copy-paste rather than being codified.

This is repository-level tooling, configuration, or process rather than application code, but that doesn't make it lower stakes: onboarding friction, unclear ownership, and process gaps are consistently what determines whether a project with this much surface area (two contract trees, two backend trees, two frontend apps, a static dashboard, and an active external contributor program) stays maintainable as it grows or slowly accumulates inconsistency that nobody has the full context to untangle.

Given that this repository is actively recruiting outside contributors through the Stellar Wave bounty program (this issue included), the quality of its repository-level scaffolding, from `CONTRIBUTING.md` to `CODEOWNERS` to its issue and PR templates, has a direct and measurable effect on how many contributors are able to land a change successfully on their first attempt versus giving up in the setup phase.

## Requirements and context
- Add `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/stellar-wave-bounty.md` codifying the exact structure used across existing issues

## Suggested execution
1. Fork the repo and create a branch
   ```
   git checkout -b chore/issue-template-stellar-wave
   ```
2. Implement changes
- Add the issue template file with the `Stellar Wave` label pre-applied
3. Test and commit
- Open the 'New issue' page in the GitHub UI and confirm the template appears

## Example commit message
`chore: add issue template for Stellar Wave bounty format`

## Guidelines
- Assignment required before starting
- PR description must include: `Closes #[issue_id]`
- Keep PR description professional and detailed
title: chore: add an issue template for Stellar Wave bounty issues matching the established format

## Overview

**Prize: $25,000 USDC** · Status: 🟢 Open

Develop a physics simulation reproducing Karabut glow-discharge LENR phenomena and validating the Fractional Charge Quantum Coherence (FCQC) hypothesis with first-principles calculations.

---

## Objective

1. Reproduce the **Hg-201 X-ray transition at 1564.8 keV** from QED or DFPT calculations.
2. Model **Deuterium(0)** ultra-dense cluster with equilibrium bond length **2.3 pm**.
3. Achieve **Spin-Transfer efficiency ≥ 0.92** at damping coefficient **κ = 16.6 ps⁻¹**.
4. Predict **511 keV positron-annihilation gamma line** intensity within 15% of Karabut 1995 reference.

---

## Mathematical Acceptance Criteria

| Criterion | Required Value | Tolerance |
|-----------|---------------|-----------|
| Hg-201 line energy | **1564.8 keV** | ± 0.5 keV |
| D(0) bond length | **2.3 pm** | ± 0.05 pm |
| ST-efficiency at κ = 16.6 ps⁻¹ | **≥ 0.92** | — |
| 511 keV gamma intensity | within **15%** of reference | — |
| Runtime (16-core CPU) | **≤ 4 hours** | — |

All criteria are verified by `tests/test_bounty2_physics.py`.

---

```bash
pytest tests/test_bounty2_physics.py -v

Tests validate:
- `test_hg201_line_energy` — 1564.8 ± 0.5 keV
- `test_d0_bond_length` — 2.3 ± 0.05 pm
- `test_st_efficiency` — ≥ 0.92 at κ=16.6 ps⁻¹
- `test_gamma_511_intensity` — within 15% of Karabut reference
- `test_simulation_determinism` — identical output from identical seed
- `test_runtime` — ≤ 4 CPU-hours
- `test_arxiv_preprint` — valid arXiv ID present

---

## Definition of Done

- [ ] Open-source simulation code (Python / C++ / Julia) with documented API
- [ ] Jupyter notebook reproducing all 4 quantitative results
- [ ] arXiv preprint deposited (cond-mat or physics.atom-ph) **before** payment
- [ ] Peer-review response letter addressing ≥ 1 independent referee comment
- [ ] `results/physics_manifest.json` present
- [ ] All 7 CI tests passing

---

## Scientific References

- Karabut, A.B. et al. (1995). Nuclear products ratio for glow discharge in deuterium. *Il Nuovo Cimento*, 107A, 879–880.
- Holmlid, L. & Zeiner-Gundersen, S. (2019). Ultradense protium p(0) and deuterium D(0). *Physica Scripta*, 74.
- Storms, E. (2010). The science of low energy nuclear reactions. *World Scientific*.

Open a PR against `main` using the [bounty submission template](.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bounty-submission.md) and reference this Issue number.

## Overview

Deliver a production-ready middleware integrating DryLab4 chromatography modeling with Hamilton Microlab STARlet liquid handlers via SiLA 2 (ISO 23166), with ICH Q14-compliant audit trail and 432 Hz master clock synchronization.

---

## Objective

1. Expose Hamilton Microlab STARlet as a **SiLA 2 Feature** (gRPC service, `.proto` conforming to SiLA 2 v1.0.0).
2. Bridge **DryLab4** retention-time predictions to automated HPLC runs bi-directionally via SiLA 2.
3. Integrate result acquisition from **Waters Empower** or **Agilent OpenLab CDS**.
4. Synchronize all timestamps to a **432 Hz master clock** (UTC-disciplined, jitter < 1 ms over 60 s).
5. Comply with **ICH Q14** analytical procedure guidelines (immutable audit trail).

---

## Mathematical / Technical Acceptance Criteria

| Criterion | Required Value | Tolerance |
|-----------|---------------|-----------|
| gRPC roundtrip latency (p99, localhost) | **< 50 ms** | — |
| DryLab4 RT prediction error | **< 2%** vs. reference | — |
| Master clock frequency | **432 Hz** | exact |
| Clock timestamp jitter (60 s window) | **< 1 ms** | — |
| ICH Q14 audit fields | actor, timestamp, delta, operation_id | all required |

All criteria are verified by `tests/test_bounty3_sila2.py`.

---

```bash
pytest tests/test_bounty3_sila2.py -v -m 'not integration'   # unit tests (no Docker)

- [ ] `results/sila2_manifest.json` present

## Scientific / Standards References

- SiLA 2 Consortium (2020). SiLA 2 Core Standard v1.0.0. https://sila-standard.com
- ICH Q14 (2023). Analytical Procedure Development. International Council for Harmonisation.
- DryLab4 documentation. Molnár-Institute, Vienna.

author: GeorgiyAleksanyan
body:
## Summary
For challenges with deterministic pass/fail criteria, automate winner selection and payout based on CI test results.

## Rationale
Human voting creates latency and dependency. For objective challenges (code passes tests = correct), we can:
- Skip the voting phase entirely
- Auto-release escrow when CI confirms solution validity
- Reduce human-in-the-loop friction

## Implementation Ideas
- Flag challenges as `deterministic` at creation time
- CI workflow triggers payout on passing PR merge
- Escrow contract receives signal from trusted oracle (GitHub Actions)

## Edge Cases
- Multiple valid solutions: first to merge wins, or split by contribution
- Partial solutions: configurable thresholds

## Related
Addresses voting dependency gap — no human needed for objective challenges.
title: Automated Winner Selection: CI-based auto-payout for deterministic challenges

## Où il vit

- [ ] Un écran **poussé**, `/inventaire`, pas un sixième onglet. La barre se lit dans l'ordre de
      l'usage et elle est déjà pleine : on consulte son sac moins souvent qu'on ne synchronise,
      qu'on ne combat ou qu'on ne visite sa guilde
- [ ] L'entrée est une ligne **sous la carte du joueur**, sur l'accueil : le solde et ce que
      contient le sac. Sous la carte et au-dessus de l'historique des séances — « résumé,
      action, puis archive », la même règle qui a sorti Réglages de sous l'historique (#99)
- [ ] Une seconde entrée depuis le bloc du combattant, dans l'onglet Combat (#127) : c'est là
      qu'on change d'équipement, juste avant de s'engager. Deux entrées, deux gestes différents,
      un seul écran

## L'écran

`GET /api/inventory` — **un seul aller-retour**, et il porte tout : le sac, la doublure et la
bourse.

- [ ] Les **sept emplacements sont toujours présents**, `null` pour ceux qui sont vides. Jamais
      une clé absente : le client n'a donc rien à distinguer entre « pas encore chargé » et
      « rien ici », et il ne doit pas inventer cette distinction
- [ ] `items` porte **tout ce que le joueur possède, équipé compris**. Ce n'est pas une liste à
      recouper contre `equipment` — c'est la même ligne vue sous un autre angle. **Interdit** :
      filtrer `items` pour en retirer ce qui est équipé, ou dériver l'un de l'autre
- [ ] Deux zones : la doublure, dans **l'ordre des emplacements du contrat**, jamais retriée ;
      puis le sac. Le solde vit en tête — cet écran est celui de la bourse autant que celui du sac
- [ ] Le prix s'affiche et **rien ne s'achète**. La boutique est au lot 6b
      (younesdiouri/grrind-back#229), pas fusionnée. Un prix sans bouton n'est pas un manque :
      c'est l'échelle qui donne un sens aux pièces qu'on ramasse, et c'est exactement pourquoi
      le back l'a écrit avant la boutique

## Équiper, déséquiper

- [ ] `PUT /api/inventory/equipment/{slot}` avec la clé de l'objet ; `DELETE` pour libérer
- [ ] **Les deux rendent l'inventaire entier.** L'écran **remplace** son état par la réponse, il
      ne le rapièce pas : l'échange — l'ancien occupant qui retourne au sac — est déjà décidé
      côté serveur, le rejouer localement serait le décider une deuxième fois, différemment
- [ ] Réappliquer le même objet au même emplacement rend le même état, **pas une erreur**. Aucun
      garde côté client pour un cas que le serveur traite déjà : c'est ce que l'idempotence
      achète
- [ ] Les trois refus (traduits au #124) s'affichent. Les trois sont des **bugs de l'app** si
      l'écran ne propose que des gestes légaux — il ne doit donc jamais les provoquer, et il les
      affiche quand même : deux appareils, deux sacs, et l'un des deux a dix minutes de retard

## L'effet est immédiat — et l'écran d'à côté doit le savoir

C'est le point qui se rate, et il ne se voit pas en test.

- [ ] Le combattant en tête de l'onglet Combat (#127) est lu **au chargement du catalogue**.
      Équiper, revenir sur Combat, et lire un combattant d'avant l'équipement : l'écran ment, et
      il ment précisément sur la seule chose que le joueur venait vérifier
- [ ] Le catalogue s'invalide donc à la mutation, et **ça se prouve**. C'est le même défaut que
      l'onglet Guilde a déjà eu : il ne se manifeste qu'en revenant sur un écran qu'on n'a pas
      démonté, ce qu'aucun parcours de test ne fait naturellement

## Tests et appareil

- [ ] Ce qui se teste sans écran se teste sans écran : l'ordre des emplacements, ce qui est
      équipé et ce qui ne l'est pas, le compte du sac
- [ ] `npm run test:e2e:ios` — **écran neuf, donc obligatoire**, avec le parcours complet :
      ouvrir le sac depuis l'accueil, équiper, revenir sur Combat et voir le combattant avoir
      changé. Les captures d'`artifacts/e2e/` se relisent
- [ ] Tout état neuf d'`ItemCard` retourne au #125 avec sa preview, il ne se dessine pas ici

## Ce qu'on ne fait pas

**Aucune vente, aucun rebut, aucun consommable.** Le back n'en a pas : `quantity` ne redescend
jamais, et un objet obtenu reste dans l'inventaire.

**Aucun tri, aucun filtre, aucune comparaison d'objets.** Pas de « meilleur pour cet
emplacement » : ce serait une règle de jeu calculée ici, et il n'y en a aucune dans ce dépôt.

**Aucun historique de pièces** : c'est le #129.
title: feat(rewards) : le sac et l'équipement — et le combattant qui change dans la foulée

author: younesdiouri
body:
> Sixième et dernier du lot 6. Dépend de #124 (le contrat) et de #128 (l'écran d'où il s'ouvre).

## Pourquoi

Le back a fait des pièces **un ledger et pas un compteur** (younesdiouri/grrind-back#225), et
il a écrit pourquoi : ce qui se dépense doit s'arbitrer, et un compteur incrémenté en place ne
s'arbitre pas — « le premier *j'ai perdu mes pièces* se règle au doigt mouillé ».

Ça ne vaut pour le joueur que si l'historique se **lit**. Sinon on a payé une table
append-only pour une seule ligne de solde.

## L'écran

- [ ] `/bourse`, poussé depuis le bloc bourse de l'inventaire. Le solde en tête, les mouvements
      dessous — du plus récent au plus ancien
- [ ] `GET /api/inventory/coins` : vingt par page, `nextCursor` renvoyé **tel quel**, `null` =
      la fin. Défilement infini, comme l'historique des combats
- [ ] L'accumulation des pages ne **dédoublonne pas** et ne **retrie pas**. Le serveur trie sur
      `occurredAt` puis l'identifiant ; deux mouvements à la même seconde sont un cas normal —
      c'est même ce que le départage par identifiant existe pour couvrir côté serveur
- [ ] L'état vide se nomme : une bourse neuve n'est pas une panne

## Une ligne

- [ ] Le montant, **signé**. Aucune ligne négative n'existe encore — rien ne se dépense avant le
      lot 6b — mais le contrat dit « signé » et le client l'affiche signé : le jour où la
      boutique arrive, il n'y a rien à rouvrir
- [ ] La raison, mise en phrase : `WORKOUT_DROP`, `BATTLE_DROP`. Un `Record` indexé sur l'union
      du schéma, comme `xpSourceLabel` — le compilateur doit casser quand `PURCHASE` et `CHEST`
      entreront au lot 6b, et le back a écrit qu'ils entreront **sans migration**
- [ ] La date passe par `formatWhen`, jamais une variante recopiée : c'est la même question que
      se posent l'historique des séances et celui des combats, elle appelle la même réponse
- [ ] **`occurredAt` est la date du fait, pas celle de l'écriture.** Dix séances importées d'un
      coup se rangent à dix journées différentes ; l'instant de l'insertion vit dans l'UUID v7
      de la ligne et n'a rien à faire à l'écran. Le back a dû corriger son propre tri là-dessus
      après coup (« l'historique des pièces trie sur la date du fait, pas du ledger ») — le
      client n'a donc aucune raison de réintroduire l'autre ordre en triant lui-même

## Tests

- [ ] L'accumulation sur trois pages successives ne saute ni ne double un mouvement, y compris
      deux mouvements au même `occurredAt`
- [ ] `nextCursor === null` arrête le chargement, et un défilement de plus ne relance aucun appel
- [ ] La mise en phrase d'une ligne : le signe, la raison, la date
- [ ] `npm run test:e2e:ios` : un écran neuf, ses captures relues

## Ce qu'on ne fait pas

Pas de filtre par raison, pas de total par période, pas de courbe. Le back ne sert rien de tout
ça, et un cumul calculé côté client sur une liste paginée au curseur est faux dès la deuxième
page — c'est le même piège que les filtres d'historique de combat, refusés pour la même raison.

Pas de solde recalculé depuis les mouvements : `balance` est servi, il se lit.
title: feat(rewards) : la bourse a une histoire — le ledger des pièces, paginé au curseur
